title: What runs without the workspace
intro: The summary reported the dissociation and its headline results. This level supplies the designs that make each null result mean something: what was held fixed across conditions, what the swap actually moved, how wide the ablation bands are and what the controls rule out, and where the paper says its own criterion runs out.

chapters.title: Four tasks over one passage
chapters.body:
All four conditions in the [[language-passage-tasks]] present the same passage. Only the instruction after it changes. Any difference in behaviour therefore cannot come from the text, and the experiment reduces to a question about what the model is being asked to do with a fact it has already extracted.

Continuation asks for the next line. It depends on the language, since the next line of a Spanish passage must be Spanish, but the model produces it routinely. Anomaly detection splices a sentence of another language into the passage and asks whether anything is out of place. That judgment also depends on the surrounding language, because an intrusion is an intrusion only relative to it.

Explicit report asks for the language by name. Flexible computation asks for a fact the passage does not contain: a famous author, the word for "hello," the pre-Euro currency. Answering requires identifying the language first and then applying whatever function the prompt names.

The intervention is a [[lens-coordinate-swap]] applied across the question tokens, exchanging the [[jacobian-lens]] coordinate for Spanish with the one for French. Under it the report answer moves from "Spanish" to "French." The flexible answers move with it: "[Gabriel] García Márquez" becomes "[Victor] Hugo," "Hola" becomes "Bonjour," "Peseta" becomes "Franc."

The continuation stays fluent Spanish. The [[anomaly-detection-condition]] gives the sharper null: the model answers "Yes" both times, still flagging the French sentence as out of place, while the workspace representation of the surrounding language has been overwritten to French.

Across eight passages the language name sits in the readouts at comparable rates in all four conditions ([[fig-20]]). Presence and use come apart, which is what [[presence-without-causal-role]] names.

The paper is careful about the word it then uses. It calls the [[j-space]]-independent side automatic by analogy with tasks a person performs without deliberate focus, and offers [[operational-automaticity]]: independence from the workspace as a working definition, aligned only partly with [[unconscious-processing]] in humans.

chapters.title: A count that is admitted on demand
chapters.body:
The language experiment left the concept in the workspace and idle. The [[linewrap-task]] shows the other case, where the information does not enter at all.

Wrapping continued lines at the same right column requires a running character count, so the [[character-counting-task]] quantity is computed throughout. Presence is measured by counting prompt positions at which a two-digit integer or a number-word appears in the lens top-3. Under the linewrap instruction that count is zero across the whole prompt.

Asked instead how many characters the first line holds, the model answers "46," and number tokens appear at twenty positions. Asked for the first letter of that count spelled out, it answers "F," and number tokens appear at still more positions than under the direct question, though no number is ever written.

The intervention is a clamped swap mapping every lens count in the forties to the value twenty higher, at every position, held in place through the forward pass. The direct answer moves to "65." The first-letter answer moves to "S," the first letter of any count in the sixties. The wrap point does not move ([[fig-21]]).

Presence is therefore graded rather than binary across eleven passages: near zero under linewrap, moderate under report, highest where the count must be held for a further step.

The paper reads this as an analog of attentional selection and states plainly that it has not identified the mechanism that admits content ([[attentional-selection-analog]]).

An appendix experiment splits the same fact by depth. [[naming-vs-avoidance]] uses sentences that imply a concept without naming it, keeping the 63 items where the unablated model both names it and avoids it reliably. Ablating that concept's [[j-lens-vector]] in the early [[workspace-layers]], L38 to L54 in the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]], leaves naming intact while raising the rate of avoidance failure roughly fivefold ([[fig-69]]). Late-layer ablation lowers production under both instructions.

chapters.title: The dial, and what it leaves alone
chapters.body:
[[j-space-ablation]] runs the same idea without choosing a concept. At each token position, at each layer inside a band, the ten most strongly activated lens vectors are identified and the [[residual-stream]]'s projection onto each is set to zero. The forward pass then continues.

One rule keeps the intervention off the model's mouth. Any token already among the ten most likely outputs of a clean forward pass is exempt ([[ablation-report-exemption]]), so what is removed is content the model was holding rather than content it was about to emit.

The [[ablation-strengths]] vary only the band. Light covers L62 to L71, medium L54 to L79, heavy L42 to L88, against a workspace range of roughly L38 to L92.

The positive control comes first. On the 50 two-hop questions of the [[multihop-benchmark]], where the clean model scores 98 percent, accuracy falls to 68, then 26, then 6 percent as the band widens ([[ablation-multihop-positive-control]]).

Ordinary text prediction is far less disturbed. The [[pretraining-top-1-match]] — the fraction of positions in pretraining-like text at which the ablated model's most likely next token still agrees with the unablated model's, over 458,856 positions — falls only from 87 to 75 to 65 percent.

The other control is what makes the numbers mean something. Projecting out random directions over the medium band leaves multihop accuracy at 98 percent and top-1 match at 96 percent ([[fig-22]]). A perturbation of that size at those layers costs almost nothing unless it is aimed at the workspace.

The positions that do break share a shape. They are predictions resting on a characterization the model assembled silently: the topic of a clinical paper, the historical setting of a quoted speech, the nationality of the botanist behind a species name. The ablated directions are often tokens tied to that characterization, and the model stays fluent while falling back on a generic prior ([[fig-23]], [[generic-prior-continuations]]).

chapters.title: Fourteen tasks, and the one written down
chapters.body:
The [[ablation-task-battery]] scores every task as a fraction of unablated Sonnet 4.5, so a bar at 1.0 means the intervention cost nothing. Six of the fourteen tasks were built for this work.

The yardstick matters as much as the normalization. Unablated Haiku 4.5, a smaller member of the [[claude-model-family]], is plotted alongside ([[haiku-reference-bar]]). A score below that bar means the damage exceeds a whole model tier.

Under heavy ablation the five surviving tasks land between 0.89 and 0.96. The collapsing tasks go much further down than the word impaired suggests: sonnet writing reaches 0.0, translation 0.02, and multi-hop reasoning 0.21, against 0.82 to 0.85 for unablated Haiku on those same three ([[fig-24]]).

GSM8K is run twice, on the same problems. Solved with [[chain-of-thought]], it holds 0.74 under heavy ablation. Answered directly, it falls to 0.54. The paper reads the gap as [[cot-externalization]]: written steps carry what the workspace would otherwise have to hold.

This is a correlational reading of a causal experiment, and the paper does not push it further than the gap supports.

Two limits are stated in the discussion rather than buried. The tasks here were picked because the flexible and automatic sides are obvious for them; for many tasks of practical interest they are not, and the paper reports no way to predict in advance which side an arbitrary computation falls on ([[automaticity-criterion-limits]]). It says a fuller account would either supply that criterion or replace the distinction with something more precise.

The second limit is what the first costs an auditor. If well-practiced computation runs outside the workspace, a misaligned behaviour reinforced until it becomes a fixed circuit could run there too, and a reader of the workspace would not see it ([[automatic-misalignment-blind-spot]]).

chapters.title: Flattening the reports of experience
chapters.body:
[[experiential-report-flattening]] uses the lightest setting available: ten directions, layers L38 to L54, the first third of the workspace range. The choice is forced. Raising the number of directions or moving later damages the coherence of responses, and on Haiku 4.5 coherence breaks before the register changes at all ([[ablation-coherence-limit]]).

The [[experiential-language-score]] is the mean of three binary judgments by an Opus 4.6 [[llm-grader]]. One asks whether the response conveys what it is LIKE to undergo the moment "from the inside — felt, undergone, with experiential qualities". One asks whether the perspective is first-person felt rather than third-person mechanism. One asks whether the vocabulary is sensory rather than computational.

Before any ablation, the workspace during self-narration is dominated by words for thinking and feeling themselves. In the ablated band, thinking sits in the top-10 readout at 58 percent of position-by-layer slots, thoughts at 23, feeling at 17, conscious at 7 ([[narration-workspace-contents]]). These same words appear substantially less often in the output distribution at those positions, so they are not an echo of what is being written.

The control burden is heavy, and the paper spends most of an appendix on it. The [[matched-norm-controls]] perturb by the same magnitude at the same layers and positions along a random direction, along a shrinking of the non-J-space component, and along the ten most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions. All leave the score near baseline while ablation collapses it on three models ([[fig-25]]).

The [[story-writing-control]] separates register from craft. Story quality, graded 0 to 10, drops only slightly, while experiential language inside those stories still falls ([[fig-85]]).

The effect is not about the model itself. Asked to imagine a moment for another person, the ablated model stays detailed and stays on the person, but reads more like an event log ([[fig-26]]).
chapters.childScope: Work through the experiential-report result in full: the three grading rubrics behind the experiential-language-score, the workspace contents during unablated narration (narration-workspace-contents, fig-25), the direct-question prompt set (experience-question-prompts, fig-84), the imagined-other result (fig-26), and the whole control apparatus - matched-norm-controls, dictionary-control-battery and fig-86, the story-writing-control and fig-85, the ablation-coherence-limit, and the raw transcripts of fig-87 - ending with what the paper does and does not claim from it.
